notes: Baseline sometimes skipped the rubric half of the deliverable entirely (vague-idea-thin) despite it being explicitly requested — skill-spec never did, across all three evals.

skill-spec's Step 5 self-evaluation caught real, concrete gaps (duplicate action items and a zero-items case in eval 0; an unstated shared-category assumption in eval 1) before the user ever saw a draft. Baseline showed no equivalent self-check in either eval.

Baseline's own from-scratch rubric for the meeting-notes eval never included a triggering-accuracy criterion at all, even though the user explicitly asked to be able to judge the skill later — this is a category skill-spec includes by design (Step 4, criterion 1) every time.

The one-off/Step-0 eval doesn't strongly differentiate the two configurations — default Claude judgment already handles an obvious one-off well on its own. The real differentiation shows up in the other two evals, where the deliverable's structure and thoroughness matter.

with_skill runs consistently took longer and used more tokens than baseline (deeper multi-round interviews, a self-evaluation pass, and a revision loop) — a deliberate tradeoff: skill-spec is optimized for a 'buildable without follow-up' deliverable, not for speed.
